cues.text: The church of Santa Pudenziana in Rome ranks among the oldest in the city, traditionally linked to a Roman senator said to have sheltered the Apostle Peter in his own household on the very ground where the church now stands.
It was here, in 1610, that a priest celebrating Mass found himself gripped by sudden doubt about the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist he held.
In the grip of that doubt, the priest lost his hold on the consecrated Host, and it fell from his hands onto the stone steps of the altar in the church's Caetani Chapel.
Rather than simply striking the stone and lying there as an ordinary wafer would, the Host is said to have left behind a distinct, visible imprint in the step itself at the point of impact.
The imprint left in the stone step of the Caetani Chapel has remained visible ever since, preserved as physical testimony to the moment.
The church was already centuries old when the event occurred, with its own long history of association with the earliest days of the Roman church.
Unlike many Eucharistic accounts built around blood, transformation, or dramatic recovery from theft or fire, the Rome 1610 account rests on something quieter.
It preserves a single mark in stone, left at the exact spot where a priest's momentary uncertainty met the object of his doubt directly underfoot.
The imprint in the Caetani Chapel remains a point of quiet devotion within a church whose foundations reach back to the apostolic age.
It is a small, specific sign layered onto ground already carrying nearly sixteen centuries of Christian memory by the time it was made.
It asks little of the visitor beyond attention to a single worn mark in old stone — evidence, for those who hold it so, that even a moment of doubt can leave something behind worth keeping.
